title: Reviews through the life cycle: gates, benefits reviews & audits
blurb: Explain the benefits of reviewing a project throughout its life cycle, from decision gates and audits to health checks and benefits reviews.
question: Eighteen months into a two-year council IT project, the sponsor asks why the project must pause for a gate review, a health check and, later, a benefits review when 'we already get monthly reports'. What are the benefits of conducting reviews throughout the life cycle?

teach.body: A review is a planned (or triggered) evaluation of a project at a point in its life cycle. Reports tell you what is happening; reviews step back and judge whether the project is still justified, on track, well managed and learning. The syllabus names decision gates, benefits reviews and audits; others include health checks, peer reviews and post-project reviews. In plain English: regular check-ups, so problems are caught while they are cheap to fix and a failing project can be stopped.

teach.h: Reviews across the extended life cycle
teach.caption: Reviews can also be triggered at any time, for example when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.

teach.body: Reviews detect problems early, while they are still cheap to fix. They test continued justification against the business case, so decisions rest on evidence rather than optimism. They create accountability, because people know their work will be examined, and they give stakeholders assurance. They capture learning for this and future projects. And they let a failing project be stopped early, freeing money and people for better uses.

teach.h: What a decision gate can decide

root.label: Decision gate
root.sub: Is the business case still sound? Are we ready?

teach.caption: Stopping a project that no longer makes sense is a success of governance, not a failure.

teach.text: Two classic traps. Sunk cost: a gate judges FUTURE costs, benefits and risks, so 'we have already spent £3m' is never a reason to continue. Outputs only: a review that asks 'was it delivered?' but not 'will the benefits still be realised?' misses its purpose. And remember: an audit checks compliance; it does not make the go or no-go decision.

teach.caption: Reports keep watch; reviews step back. A project needs both.

teach.h: Reviews in linear and iterative life cycles

rows.label: Funding
values: Fixed per time box or release

teach.body: Westshire Council is replacing its social care case system. The gate before delivery found the supplier's data migration approach untested, so delivery was approved on condition of a trial migration. A health check in month nine found the risk register three months stale; the PM fixed it within a week. An audit confirmed data protection compliance. Six months after go-live, a benefits review showed only 40% of social workers using the mobile app, so the sponsor funded extra training.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the review, then say what it checks, e.g. 'A decision gate re-tests the business case before more funding is released.'
Give the benefit and its consequence: 'so a project that is no longer viable can be stopped early'.
Use the syllabus trio where you can: decision gates, benefits reviews and audits.
Mention independence for audits and assurance reviews: it is what makes their findings credible.
Link to the life cycle: phase-end gates in linear; frequent time-box reviews in iterative.
Decision gates: go, go with conditions, hold or stop, judged on future costs, benefits and risks.
Benefits reviews: are benefits being realised? If not, corrective action. Many happen after handover.
Audits: independent checks of compliance that give assurance.
Benefits of reviews: early detection, continued justification, informed decisions, accountability, assurance, learning, stopping failing projects.
Linear: formal phase-end gates. Iterative: frequent, lighter reviews every time box.

summary: You can now explain the purpose of decision gates, benefits reviews, audits and other reviews, and the benefits they bring: early detection, continued justification, informed decisions, accountability, assurance and learning. You can also spot the sunk-cost trap and explain how reviews differ in linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate?
options: To record lessons learned after the project closes
To check that timesheets match the cost codes
To decide whether the project should continue
To confirm that all benefits have been realised
A.why: A decision gate is a go/no-go point, usually at a phase end, where the sponsor and board re-confirm the business case, readiness and funding before the next phase.

whyNot.0: Recording lessons after closure is the job of a post-project review.
whyNot.1: Checking timesheets against cost codes is routine cost control, not a gate.
whyNot.3: Most benefits are realised after handover and are checked in benefits reviews.

A.q: Which type of review independently checks whether a project is complying with agreed standards, processes and regulations?
options: An audit
A benefits review
A decision gate
A retrospective
A.why: An audit is an independent check of compliance, giving assurance that the project follows the required standards and processes.

whyNot.1: A benefits review checks whether benefits are being realised, not compliance.
whyNot.2: A decision gate decides whether to continue, change or stop.
whyNot.3: A retrospective is the team's own learning review at the end of an iteration; it is not independent.

A.q: What is the main purpose of a benefits review?
options: To release funding for the next phase
To confirm the project followed procedures
To agree the schedule for the next stage
To check benefits are being realised
A.why: Benefits reviews measure whether planned benefits are being realised and trigger corrective action if not. Many take place after handover.

whyNot.0: Releasing funding for the next phase is a decision gate's job.
whyNot.1: Confirming that procedures were followed is the role of an audit.
whyNot.2: Agreeing the next stage's schedule is part of stage planning, approved at a gate.

B.q: At a gate review, the board approves continuation 'because £3m has already been spent', although forecasts now show remaining costs exceed the remaining benefits. What is wrong?
options: The gate should have been chaired by an auditor
Past spend should not drive a forward decision
The PM should have approved it instead
Benefits should not be considered at gates
B.why: Sunk costs cannot be recovered. A gate should compare future costs, benefits and risks; if the case no longer holds, the project should be re-planned or stopped.

whyNot.0: Gate decisions belong to the sponsor and board. Auditors provide independent assurance, not gate decisions.
whyNot.2: Gate decisions sit with the sponsor and board, not the project manager.
whyNot.3: Benefits are central to every gate decision: they are what justify continuing.

B.q: Which is NOT a typical benefit of conducting reviews throughout the life cycle?
options: Problems are detected earlier
Accountability becomes clearer
Failing projects can stop early
All risks are removed entirely
B.why: Reviews help manage risk, but no review can eliminate it. Uncertainty remains throughout a project.

whyNot.0: Early detection of problems is a core benefit of reviews.
whyNot.1: Knowing work will be reviewed strengthens accountability.
whyNot.2: Reviews such as gates allow projects that are no longer viable to be stopped early.

B.q: On an iterative app project, where do frequent reviews most typically happen?
options: At the end of each time box, with users
At one gate when the whole build is done
Once a year, alongside the financial audit
Only when the sponsor asks for an exception
B.why: Iterative life cycles build in frequent, lighter reviews: time-box reviews where users see the work, and retrospectives where the team learns.

whyNot.1: A single gate at the end resembles a linear approach and loses the early feedback iterative working relies on.
whyNot.2: An annual review is far too infrequent for time-boxed delivery.
whyNot.3: Exception reviews are triggered when tolerances are threatened; they are not the routine rhythm.

C.q: A project passed every gate on time and closed on budget, but a year later the expected benefits have not appeared. What most likely went wrong with its reviews?
options: Too many audits slowed down the delivery
Health checks were done by independent staff
The post-project review was held too soon
Gates checked outputs, not future benefits
C.why: Gates that only confirm outputs were delivered, without re-testing whether benefits are still achievable and arranging benefits reviews after handover, miss the point of reviewing.

whyNot.0: Audits check compliance; they would not explain why benefits never appeared.
whyNot.1: Independence strengthens health checks rather than weakening them.
whyNot.2: The timing of lessons capture does not explain the gap; benefits needed tracking through benefits reviews.

C.q: Nine months into a two-year project, a health check finds the risk register has not been updated for three months. What is the main benefit this review has delivered?
options: It shows that the sponsor must be replaced
It proves the business case is no longer valid
It caught a control weakness while fixable
It means the project should be stopped
C.why: Early detection: the review exposed a weakness in risk control while there was still time to put it right.

whyNot.0: A stale register needs correcting; it does not justify replacing the sponsor.
whyNot.1: An out-of-date register says nothing directly about whether the business case still holds.
whyNot.3: Stopping is for projects that are no longer justified, not for fixable process lapses.

C.q: Which THREE are benefits of reviews throughout the life cycle? (1) continued justification is tested (2) decisions are better informed (3) on-time delivery is guaranteed (4) learning is captured for future projects
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
C.why: Reviews test continued justification, inform decisions and capture learning. No review can guarantee on-time delivery.

whyNot.0: Item 3 is wrong: reviews improve the odds but cannot guarantee delivery dates.
whyNot.2: Item 3 is wrong, and item 2 (better-informed decisions) is missing.
whyNot.3: Item 3 is wrong, and item 1 (testing continued justification) is missing.

reteach.title: Think of a long road trip
reteach.question: A family is driving from Cornwall to the Scottish Highlands over three days. Where do 'reviews' happen on the journey, and why do they help?

blocks.body: At each overnight stop the family decides: carry on, change route, or turn back if a relative falls ill. That is a decision gate. Halfway, a garage checks the tyres and oil whatever the driver thinks: an independent audit or health check. At the end they ask whether it was worth it and what they would do differently: a benefits review and lessons learned. Skipping the stops does not make the trip faster; it just means problems are found at 70 mph.

steps.label: Night 1 stop
steps.sub: Carry on, re-route or turn back?

steps.label: Garage check
steps.sub: Independent look at tyres and oil

steps.label: Arrival
steps.sub: Was it worth it? What would we change?

blocks.text: Pressing on 'because we've already driven 300 miles' is the sunk-cost trap. Decide on what lies ahead, not on what is already behind you.

explain.body: A go/no-go point, usually at the end of a phase. The sponsor and board re-confirm the business case, check readiness for the next phase and release funding progressively. Possible outcomes: go, go with conditions, hold or stop.

test.q: Which question sits at the heart of every decision gate?
options: Is the project still worth continuing?
Has every task been completed early?
Which supplier offered the lowest bid?
Who should be blamed for any delays?
test.why: Every gate asks whether the project is still justified and ready to proceed, based on the business case and evidence.

whyNot.1: Gates are not about finishing early; they test viability and readiness.
whyNot.2: Supplier selection is a procurement decision, not the purpose of a gate.
whyNot.3: Reviews aim to learn and decide, not to assign blame.

explain.body: Benefits reviews check whether the benefits in the business case are being realised and trigger corrective action if not. Because many benefits appear only after outputs are in use, these reviews often continue after handover, in the extended life cycle.

test.q: When do many benefits reviews take place?
options: Before the business case is drafted
Only during the Definition phase
After handover, as benefits emerge
Only at the very first decision gate
test.why: Benefits arise when outputs are used, so many benefits reviews take place after handover.

whyNot.0: There are no benefits to review before the business case exists.
whyNot.1: Benefits are planned in Definition, but they cannot yet be measured.
whyNot.3: The first gate tests the idea's viability; benefits have not yet been realised.

explain.body: An audit independently checks compliance with standards, processes and regulations. A health check gives a snapshot of how well the project is being managed. Both are forms of assurance: they give the sponsor and board confidence, and their value depends on independence from the delivery team.

test.q: What gives an audit's findings their credibility?
options: The PM writes and signs off the findings
It is independent of the delivery team
It happens only once the project closes
It is scheduled by the delivery team
test.why: Assurance, including audit, should be independent of the delivery team so its findings are objective.

whyNot.0: A PM signing off their own audit removes the independence that makes it credible.
whyNot.2: Audits can happen at any point; waiting until closure loses the chance to act.
whyNot.3: Who schedules it matters less than independence, and the delivery team controlling it weakens objectivity.

explain.body: Post-project reviews capture lessons at closure; peer reviews bring experienced eyes mid-project; retrospectives let iterative teams improve every time box. Learning is only a benefit if the lessons are applied to future work.

test.q: What is the main purpose of a post-project review?
options: To approve funding for another phase
To decide whether to stop the project
To check compliance with regulations
To capture lessons for future work
test.why: A post-project review evaluates how the project went and captures lessons so future projects improve.

whyNot.0: Approving funding is done at decision gates.
whyNot.1: Stop decisions are taken at gates during the project.
whyNot.2: Compliance checks are the role of audits.
